claims.claimText: From Semester 1 2025, the default position in the University of Sydney Academic Integrity Policy has been reversed: except for supervised examinations and supervised in-semester tests, students may use automated writing tools or generative AI to complete assessments unless expressly prohibited by the unit coordinator.

evidence.evidenceSnippet: Except for supervised examinations and supervised in-semester tests, students may use automated writing tools or generative artificial intelligence to complete assessments, unless expressly prohibited by the unit of study coordinator.
evidence.snippetLocation: Semester 1 2025 section, 'Allowable assistance' in the Academic Integrity Policy

claims.claimText: The University of Sydney's Academic Integrity Policy 2022 states it is an academic integrity breach to inappropriately generate content using artificial intelligence to complete an assessment task, and submitting an assessment generated by AI may be considered contract cheating.

evidence.evidenceSnippet: Clause 4(9)(2)(j)(i) states that it is an academic integrity breach to inappropriately generate content using artificial intelligence to complete an assessment task. Clause 4(13)(1)(i) states that submitting an assessment generated by AI may be considered contract cheating.
evidence.snippetLocation: The policy and assessment frameworks section, 'What is in the policy about generative AI use by students?'

claims.claimText: The University of Sydney has adopted a 'two-lane approach' to assessment: Lane 1 comprises secure, in-person supervised assessments to assure learning, and Lane 2 comprises open assessments that support and scaffold the use of all available and relevant tools including generative AI.

claims.claimText: University of Sydney guidance states that misusing generative AI can breach the Academic Integrity Policy 2022, with examples including using AI in assessments where prohibited, submitting AI-generated work without acknowledgment, and inputting University teaching materials or personal information into AI tools.

evidence.evidenceSnippet: Misusing AI can breach the Academic Integrity Policy 2022 . Examples of misuse include: Submitting AI-generated work without appropriate acknowledgment using AI where it has been prohibited in a 'secure' assessment type, such as during a secure exam inputting University teaching or course materials, content generated by another student, intellectual property from external partners, or any person's personal or health information.
evidence.snippetLocation: When you can and can't use AI section, Misuse of AI

claims.claimText: University of Sydney states that students who use AI in assessments are required to acknowledge it, including any tools that use generative AI such as translation tools, paraphrasing tools or referencing tools; failing to provide acknowledgement can lead to a breach of the Academic Integrity Policy 2022.

evidence.evidenceSnippet: If you use AI in your assessments, you're required to acknowledge it - this includes acknowledging any tools that use generative AI, such as translation tools, paraphrasing tools or referencing tools. You are not required to acknowledge tools used for word processing, or which only correct basic spelling and grammar. Failing to provide acknowledgement or any other misuse can lead to a breach of the Academic Integrity Policy 2022 .

claims.claimText: The University of Sydney advises that Turnitin's AI detection tool may be used if a marker suspects AI-generated work where its use was not permitted or not acknowledged, but the AI detector score would not be the only evidence relied upon for an academic integrity case.

evidence.evidenceSnippet: If a marker or teacher suspects that part or all of your assessment has been generated using AI technology and its use was not permitted, or use was not acknowledged, the Turnitin AI detection tool may be used to evaluate the situation. It's important to note that the AI detector score would not be the only evidence relied upon for an academic integrity case, but will be considered alongside other relevant evidence.

heldClaims.claimText: Historical rule (Academic Integrity Policy 2022 as described in the Teaching@Sydney FAQ): students could only use assistance, including automated writing tools, if the unit of study outline expressly permitted it. Current student guidance (updated 2 June 2026) instead allows AI in open assessments and generally prohibits it in secure assessments unless expressly permitted, so this undated prior-permission rule is held as historical and not shown as a current university-wide rule. The current Policy Register text was not re-read clause by clause.
